transcript:
"This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour."
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
A federal judge in California has denied a request by the Justice Department
to set aside thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections.
The Justice Department says it is appealing, as NPR's Jude Joffee Block reports.
The Justice Department wants to stop California election officials
from processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 individuals
that federal officials say are likely non-citizens.
California officials argued the DOJ's list is unreliable
and said the demand to set aside the ballots is infeasible.
Judge David Carter rejected the DOJ's request,
expressing concern about disenfranchising voters and potential election chaos.
He wrote if the executive branch can "discount votes and threaten an ongoing election
due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger."
Jude Joffee Block, NPR News.
Brazil's defeated presidential candidate says he's the country's true leader
and he's vowing to lead the opposition from the U.S. after arriving in Miami.
Flavio Bolsonaro and his family were granted visas by the Trump administration,
as NPR's Kerry Kahn reports.
Bolsonaro left Brazil, crossed into Argentina,
then flew to Ecuador and finally to the U.S. with his family.
He posted a letter on X declaring himself as "the true elected president of Brazil."
Not long after, he posted a new statement,
downgrading himself to the true elected leader of Brazil.
He compared himself to liberation figures Charles de Gaulle
and Maria Corina Machado of Venezuela, amongst others.
He said he would from afar lead the opposition
to incumbent President Luis Anacio Lula da Silva
and accused Brazil's judiciary of being weaponized
to politically persecute his family.
He did not provide evidence of voter fraud.
International observers have commended Brazil's election results.
Kerry Kahn, NPR News, Rio de Janeiro.
Major League Baseball has a new champion.
The Milwaukee Brewers won the World Series a short time ago,
defeating the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 to win the series in five games.
Steve Futterman was there.
For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions.
Right now, the Brewers mobbing one another on the pitcher's mound.
A huge celebration.
Game five was pretty much controlled from start to finish by the Brewers.
For the Brewers franchise that began play in 1969,
this ends decades of frustrations and near misses.
Next up, the victory parade in Milwaukee.
For NPR News, I'm Steve Futterman at the World Series in St. Petersburg, Florida.
The Golden State Valkyries could clinch their first WNBA title Thursday.
The Valkyries lead the series against the Atlanta Dream, three games to two.
Game six is a sellout, despite an early afternoon tip-off in Atlanta.
This is NPR News.
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warr says the overall economic picture looks good,
but inflation remains too high.
Quashing inflation is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar.
Same way it's not about some isolated data point.
If it were about those two things, this job would be easier,
and we wouldn't be suffering from nearly six years of inflation above target.
Warr speaking during his press conference following Wednesday's policy meeting
in which the Fed held interest rates steady, as widely expected.
Two days after the federal government sued Utah to stop its case against prediction market app Kalshi,
the state has filed criminal charges from member station KUER Hugo Ricard Bell reports.
Utah's Attorney General filed 13 charges and a misdemeanor against Kalshi.
They include one second-degree felony count of a patent of unlawful criminal activity,
12 counts of online gambling promotion, and one misdemeanor count of general gambling promotion.
Earlier this year, Utah's neighbor Arizona filed 20 criminal charges against the app.
A federal judge initially blocked that case,
but it's since been potentially revived after a 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruling.
In a statement, Kalshi called the Utah charges "a crazy overreach."
Utah is clearly playing politics.
We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona.
For NPR News, I'm Hugo Ricard Bell in Salt Lake City.
